passage: The hostel mess shut for the festival week, and Sunaina had 410 rupees left with nine days to go. She sat cross-legged on her bed with her phone, scrolling the month's bank statement line by line while her roommate Simran boiled water for tea. No single big buy showed up. Instead the same items repeated: a food delivery at night, another at lunch, a video subscription, a music subscription, a cloud storage fee she had forgotten. She copied each into a notebook and added them up. The total made her stop chewing her pen. "Simran, come look. It's all these small ones." They cancelled the two subscriptions she never used, bought rice, lentils and eggs from the corner shop, and Sunaina wrote a daily limit on a sticky note above her desk. On day nine she still had forty rupees.

qa.q: How many days did Sunaina have to get through when the hostel mess shut?
qa.a: Sunaina had nine days to go, with 410 rupees left.

qa.q: What was Sunaina feeling when the total made her stop chewing her pen?
qa.a: Shocked and uneasy, because the small food and subscription spends added up to far more than she expected.

qa.q: What could Sunaina keep doing next month so small spends do not surprise her?
qa.a: She could keep a daily limit, glance at the statement every week and cancel any subscription she is not using.

qa.q: How might Simran have felt when Sunaina called out for help looking at the list?
qa.a: Simran probably felt concerned and ready to help, since Simran came to look and joined in cancelling the two subscriptions. 🙂

grounding: Shows a student running short before month end and finding that small repeated food and subscription spends add up.

passage: On the 24th, Kiran's phone buzzed with a low-balance message, and salary day was still six days away. At lunch in the studio pantry he stared at the screen. Rent, phone bill and metro pass were already paid, so where had it gone? Kunal, from the next desk, slid over a pen. "Open the transactions and read them out." Kiran read: coffee, delivery, cab, delivery, a game pass, delivery. Kunal tallied on a napkin. Delivery meals alone came to nearly a third of the pay. "No single splurge," Kunal said. "Just forty here, sixty there." That evening Kiran packed a tiffin for the coming week and set a monthly limit for delivery in a note on his phone. The next month, on the 24th, he checked the balance and it was still healthy.

qa.q: On which day of the month did Kiran's low-balance message arrive?
qa.a: It arrived on the 24th, with salary day still six days away.

qa.q: What might Kiran have been worried about while staring at the screen in the pantry?
qa.a: Kiran was anxious and puzzled about where the money had gone, since rent, phone bill and metro pass were already paid.

qa.q: What steps that evening turned Kiran's confusion into a plan?
qa.a: Kiran packed a tiffin for the coming week and set a monthly limit for delivery meals in a phone note.

qa.q: Why might Kunal have asked Kiran to read the transactions aloud?
qa.a: Kunal probably wanted Kiran to notice the repeated delivery spends, and the napkin tally made the pattern visible. 🙂

grounding: Shows a first-job earner running out of money before payday because repeated small delivery and game spends outweighed any single purchase.

passage:
Note from the hostel office, Tuesday.
Noor knocked on my door on the twenty-third and asked to borrow enough for a bus pass. She said she had "bought nothing big this month" and looked honestly puzzled. I did not lend it straight away. Instead we sat at my table and she opened her payment history. Step one, we wrote down every spend over the month. Step two, we circled the repeats. There were nineteen late-night food orders, a music plan, a video plan and a study-notes subscription she had forgotten. No single item was large. Together they came to more than her mess fees. Noor went quiet, then laughed a little and said, "It was the samosas at midnight." Step three, she cancelled two subscriptions while sitting there. I lent the bus fare and we agreed she would come back on the first to plan the next month.
Nikita, hostel warden

qa.q: On which date did Noor knock on the warden's door?
qa.a: Noor knocked on the door on the twenty-third.

qa.q: How did Noor feel when the circled repeats were added up?
qa.a: Noor felt embarrassed and a bit stunned: she went quiet, then laughed a little and admitted it was the midnight samosas.

qa.q: Which step in Nikita's note helped Noor most, and why?
qa.a: Writing down every spend and circling the repeats helped most, because it showed that many small orders, not one big buy, had emptied the month.

qa.q: What would change if Nikita had simply lent the money at the door?
qa.a: Noor would have got through the week but still not known where the money went, so the same gap could open again next month.

grounding: Illustrates a student who runs short before month end and discovers that small repeated food orders and forgotten subscriptions added up.

passage:
26th, night.
Balance: almost nothing, and payday is five days away. Afreen saw my face at dinner and said, "Trisha, you keep checking that app like it will change." It won't. I have not bought a single big thing since my first salary came. No phone, no shoes, nothing. So where did it go?
I finally scrolled through the whole month. Chai and a sandwich delivered to the office every afternoon, because the canteen line is long. Three streaming plans, one of them from a free trial I never cancelled. Two cab rides a week when I was "too tired" for the metro. Each one felt like nothing.
I wrote them all in the back of this diary and added them up twice. Tomorrow I will cancel two plans and ask Afreen if we can cook on weekdays. Feeling foolish, but also a bit less lost.

qa.q: What did Trisha have delivered to the office every afternoon?
qa.a: Chai and a sandwich were delivered to the office every afternoon.

qa.q: What was Trisha feeling after adding up the month?
qa.a: Trisha felt foolish about the small spends but also a bit less lost, because the gap finally made sense.

qa.q: What small step could Trisha take next month to catch this earlier?
qa.a: Trisha could glance at the spends every week instead of at month end, and cancel any free trial before it turns into a plan.

qa.q: How might Afreen see Trisha's habit of checking the app?
qa.a: Afreen notices the worry and gently teases it, and may be glad to cook together if Trisha asks.

grounding: Shows a first-job earner who has made no big purchase yet runs short, and traces it to daily deliveries, forgotten plans and cabs.

passage: Vikas had been a clerk at the cooperative bank in Sirsi for exactly one month, and on the 22nd his phone showed a balance that wouldn't cover the bus pass. "Where did it go?" he asked Chaitanya at the tea stall outside the bank. "I bought one thing. The shoes." Chaitanya took the phone and scrolled through the payment history slowly, the way the bank had taught them to check a ledger. Shoes, once. Then the evening snack order from the delivery app, nineteen times. A video subscription, a music subscription and a cricket-streaming pass he'd forgotten about. Chai and samosa, almost daily. Two mobile recharges. "The shoes aren't your problem," Chaitanya said. "This is." He tapped the long column of small amounts. Vikas stared at it. Not one of them had felt like spending. Together they looked like the whole salary.

qa.q: How many times had Vikas ordered the evening snack from the delivery app?
qa.a: Nineteen times.

qa.q: How did Vikas feel looking at the long column of small amounts?
qa.a: He was confused and dismayed, since he had blamed the shoes and none of the small payments had felt like spending.

qa.q: What could Vikas do before next month's salary is gone?
qa.a: He could go through the list with Chaitanya, stop the subscriptions he had forgotten, and keep an eye on the small daily payments as they happen.

qa.q: How does Chaitanya see the problem?
qa.a: Chaitanya sees it plainly and kindly, checking the history like a ledger and pointing out that the pile of small amounts matters more than the one big buy.

grounding: Shows a first-job earner who runs out of money before the month ends and discovers that small repeated orders and forgotten subscriptions, not one purchase, used it up.
